bullets: Economic activity in San Marino has remained resilient with stabilizing growth and record employment in 2024, despite a regional slowdown and high interest rates.
Real GDP growth slowed to 0.4 percent in 2023 due to weakening external demand, but is projected to pick up gradually to 1.3 percent in 2025.
Headline inflation declined significantly to 1.2 percent in July 2024 and is expected to remain low at 2.0 percent in 2025.
The central government primary balance reached 2.4 percent of GDP in 2023, while public debt declined to 68 percent of GDP in 2024.
Staff recommend an additional fiscal consolidation of 1 percent of GDP over the next three years to firmly place public debt on a downward path below the 60 percent target.
In the banking sector, non-performing loan ratios dropped sharply from 53 to 21 percent following securitization via an Asset Management Company and large write-offs.
Despite improved liquidity and reported profits in 2023, the banking sector remains vulnerable due to high operating costs, limited income-generating assets, and tight capitalization in some banks.
Key downside risks identified by staff include lingering weakness in external demand, tighter than expected global monetary conditions, and remaining domestic financial sector vulnerabilities.
executive_summary.balance_of_risks: Risks to San Marino's economic outlook are tilted to the downside, primarily stemming from potential external demand shocks and domestic financial and fiscal vulnerabilities.

section_summaries.title: Press Release and Selected Indicators
section_summaries.summary: San Marino's economy remains resilient with stabilizing activity and record employment, supported by strong service performance offsetting manufacturing declines, while inflation dropped below 2 percent. Executive Directors endorsed the staff appraisal, noting a stronger fiscal position with a 2023 primary balance of 2.4 percent of GDP, improved bank liquidity, and significant NPL reductions through an Asset Management Company and calendar provisioning. However, the report highlights the need for further fiscal consolidation, cost reductions in banks, and structural reforms to lift potential growth.

section_summaries.title: CONTEXT: A UNIQUE OPPORTUNITY FOR REFORMS
section_summaries.summary: San Marino transitioned to a new growth model led by manufacturing and export services after the Global Financial Crisis shrank its oversized banking sector by 80 percent. Despite this resilience, high public debt at 68 percent of GDP and limited countercyclical buffers remain vulnerabilities. A recently negotiated EU association agreement offers opportunities for deeper integration and reforms, supported by a newly elected stable government coalition holding about three-quarters of parliament seats.

section_summaries.title: RECENT DEVELOPMENTS
section_summaries.summary: Economic growth slowed to 0.4 percent in 2023 due to declining external demand and manufacturing contraction, though solid services growth kept unemployment low at 3.9 percent. The current account surplus remained high at 13.9 percent of GDP, and inflation dropped to 1.2 percent by July 2024. The fiscal position exceeded expectations with a primary balance net of bank support reaching 2.4 percent of GDP in 2023, while NPL securitization and write-offs significantly reduced the NPL ratio from 53 to 21 percent.

section_summaries.title: OUTLOOK AND RISKS
section_summaries.summary: Economic growth is projected to pick up to 1.3 percent in 2025 as external demand and real wages improve, with inflation returning to 2 percent. The public debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to decline gradually from 68 percent in 2024 to 62 percent by 2028. Downside risks include external conflicts, euro area slowdowns, and domestic financial contingencies, whereas faster implementation of the EU association agreement provides an upside.

section_summaries.title: POLICY AGENDA: STRENGTHENING THE FRAMEWORK TO COPE WITH SHOCKS — A. Strengthening the Fiscal Position
section_summaries.summary: San Marino must implement an additional fiscal consolidation of 1 percent of GDP over the next three years to reduce debt below 60 percent of GDP. Key measures include introducing a value-added tax, broadening the income tax base, rationalizing spending and interest subsidies, and keeping public wage and pension growth below inflation. Upgrading debt management capacity is also essential to manage refinancing risks ahead of the 2027 Eurobond amortization.

section_summaries.title: B. Finalizing the Banking Reform to Safeguard Stability
section_summaries.summary: Despite progress in reducing NPL ratios to 21 percent via the Asset Management Company, San Marino's banking system remains vulnerable due to high operating costs, limited income-generating assets, and tight capitalization. Banks must urgently adjust operating costs to match regional peers, lift shareholding limits, and address potential capital needs transparently. Furthermore, the central bank needs strengthened financial autonomy to implement EU regulatory standards.

section_summaries.title: C. Implement Structural Reforms to Support Broad-Based Growth
section_summaries.summary: The upcoming ratification of the EU association agreement offers significant opportunities to boost productivity, enhance public administration, and accelerate structural reforms. Key priorities include increasing labor market flexibility by removing restrictions on cross-border hiring, safeguarding energy security, and reforming the real estate market to support NPL resolution. Additionally, San Marino continues improving its macroeconomic statistics with IMF support.

section_summaries.title: STAFF APPRAISAL
section_summaries.summary: San Marino's economy remains resilient with positive growth driven by strong services and robust employment, while the external position is broadly in line with fundamentals. However, staff recommends an additional fiscal consolidation of 1 percent of GDP over three years to reduce public debt below 60 percent. Financial sector vulnerabilities require accelerated cost adjustments in banks, faster increases in risk weights for junior securities, and enhanced debt management capacity to handle the 2027 Eurobond maturity.

section_summaries.title: I. Risk Assessment Matrix
section_summaries.summary: The risk assessment matrix highlights high external risks from regional conflicts and global growth slowdowns, alongside domestic risks from delayed fiscal consolidation and slow banking system restructuring. Key policy responses involve accelerating fiscal and structural reforms, maintaining high liquid buffers, and extending central bank powers to handle failing banks.

section_summaries.title: II. Authorities’ Response to Past IMF Recommendations
section_summaries.summary: The Sammarinese authorities have made notable progress in addressing past IMF recommendations, including establishing an Asset Management Company, initiating calendar provisioning, retaining bank profits to bolster capital, and completing negotiations for the EU association agreement. Additionally, the government published its first medium-term fiscal strategy and increased staffing in the debt management office.

section_summaries.title: III. External Sector Assessment
section_summaries.summary: San Marino's external position in 2023 was broadly in line with fundamentals and desirable policies, supported by a strong current account surplus of 14 percent of GDP driven by robust manufacturing and tourism exports. Gross international reserves increased to 740 million euros, covering about 110 percent of the ARA metric. Competitiveness has recovered through moderate wage growth, although structural gaps in business regulations remain.

section_summaries.title: IV. Sovereign Risk and Debt Sustainability Assessment
section_summaries.summary: Public debt is projected to decline to 68 percent of GDP at the end of 2024 and decrease slowly over the medium term, supported by robust nominal growth and primary surpluses. Medium-term risks are assessed as moderate, though gross financing needs will spike to 23 percent of GDP in 2027 due to Eurobond amortization. Rebuilding fiscal buffers and improving debt management capacity are vital to mitigate rollover and refinancing risks.

section_summaries.title: V. San Marino Asset Management Company
section_summaries.summary: In December 2023, San Marino transferred 611 million euros of gross NPLs to a newly launched Asset Management Company, reducing the NPL ratio significantly. The senior tranches carry a government guarantee and were sold abroad, while mezzanine and junior tranches remain on bank balance sheets. As of June 2024, NPL recovery has exceeded expectations, reaching 26.3 million euros primarily through loan restructurings.

section_summaries.title: VI. Implementation of the VAT in San Marino: Insights from Recent FAD TA Report
section_summaries.summary: Introducing a 15 percent standard rate Value Added Tax (VAT) will modernize San Marino's indirect tax system, replace the single-stage Monofase tax, and align procedures with international standards while generating net revenues of about 0.8 percent of GDP. Successful implementation requires careful transition planning, strong anti-fraud measures, stakeholder engagement, and technological upgrades to core IT tax administration systems.

section_summaries.title: VII. Data Issues
section_summaries.summary: The data provided to the Fund has some shortcomings but remains broadly adequate for surveillance. While national accounts, external sector, and monetary statistics comply with international standards, certain fiscal and real sector statistics suffer from publication delays. The authorities are actively addressing these data gaps through ongoing cooperation with IMF statistical experts.

section_summaries.title: Informational Annex
section_summaries.summary: San Marino has been a member of the IMF since September 1992 and uses the euro as its official currency under an agreement with the European Union. The country maintains an exchange system free of restrictions on current international transactions and participates in the Enhanced General Data Dissemination System. Technical assistance from the IMF has historically focused on statistics, tax policy, banking restructuring, and AML/CFT frameworks.
